transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, doctor... it’s, uh, it’s a lot, to be honest. I guess I’ll try to start from where it makes sense. I’ve been an electrician for over twenty years now. Started right after I did a couple years of college and realized sitting in a lecture hall wasn't for me. I’ve wired up hundreds of houses, commercial buildings, you name it. I know the codes, I know the safety protocols inside and out. I'm the guy people call when they want it done right and done safe. 

But... well, I came in today because I just can't shake this one thought. It's just sitting there in my head, constantly. I keep thinking that if all my years of training, all my experience as an electrician couldn't keep my own brother safe... then I'm a danger to anybody who works with me. Or even anybody who lives under my own roof. 

I mean, if I couldn't protect my own flesh and blood with the one thing I'm supposed to be an absolute expert in, how can I trust myself around my crew? How can I even fix a simple breaker in my own house without feeling like I'm putting everyone I care about in jeopardy? It just goes round and round in my head, and I can't seem to get past it, no matter how many times I check my work or go over the safety manuals. I just feel like a walking hazard, you know? Like it's only a matter of time before I hurt someone else, and I just don't know how to live with that hanging over me every time I pick up my tools.
Can you tell me more about this thought? Specifically, does it come into your mind uninvited, and do you feel it's something you can't control?

Yeah, uninvited doesn't even begin to cover it, doc. It’s... it’s not like I’m sitting around trying to dwell on it or punishing myself on purpose, you know? It just completely hijacks me. I could be having a perfectly normal Tuesday, just doing my job. Like, I'll be in the middle of wiring a panel—a standard 200-amp subpanel, something I've done literally a thousand times. I’ve got my wire strippers in my hand, I'm checking the phase tape, making sure the lugs are torqued down perfectly because, like I said, I don't mess around with safety. 

But then, out of nowhere, it's like the whole job site just drops out from under me. The concrete floor, the tools, the guys talking in the background—it all just vanishes. And suddenly I'm right back there. I can literally smell the smoke. That awful, acrid, burning electrical smoke that gets stuck right in the back of your throat, and... and I see my brother. I just see him. It’s so real I can barely breathe, and I'm just frozen there with my tools. 

And it’s not just at work, either. I can't even escape it at home. My nephew—he's a good kid, he lives with me now—he'll just be coming inside and he'll shut the garage door. Just a normal, everyday sound, right? The metal tracks clanking and the heavy wood hitting the cement. But the second I hear that slam, boom, it happens all over again. The smell of the smoke, seeing my brother, the whole thing just washing over me. I try to shake my head, I try to focus on whatever is right in front of me, like the kitchen counter or the TV, but I absolutely cannot control it. It just takes over my entire reality, no matter how hard I try to fight it off or tell myself I'm safe.
Have you found yourself avoiding certain places, people, or activities because they remind you of what happened to your brother?

Well... yeah. Yeah, absolutely. I mean, it's gotten to the point where I have to plan my whole day around trying not to run into things that set it off, which is... it's exhausting, honestly. Take my own house, for example. My garage. I used to spend every weekend in there. I had a whole setup, you know? Workbench, all my tools organized on pegboards, a little fridge for beers... it was my sanctuary. But now? I don't go in my own garage unless I absolutely have to. Like, if the water heater goes out and I have no choice, I'll run in, fix it as fast as humanly possible, and get the hell out. I can't stand being in there. The smell of the oil, the concrete floor, the way the light hits the tools... it's just too much. It's like standing on the edge of a cliff, just waiting for the ground to give way. 

And it's not just the garage. I used to volunteer down at my church, doing all their electrical maintenance. Changing out the old fluorescent ballasts in the fellowship hall, running new lines for the AV equipment, making sure the exit signs were up to code... I liked doing it, giving back, you know? But I had to quit. I just told the pastor I didn't have the time anymore, which was a lie, but how do you explain that looking at a junction box in a basement makes you feel like you're going to throw up? I couldn't handle being around the wiring, the smell of the old insulation... I just couldn't do it. 

Even just talking to people is hard now. Guys on the crew, they're always talking about their weekends, right? Rebuilding an engine, working on some old muscle car... my brother and I used to do that. We were always tinkering with cars. So if one of the guys starts talking about a car project, or... God forbid, if someone brings up the fire, or anything even remotely related to it, I just shut them down fast. I'll walk away, change the subject, put my headphones on, whatever it takes. I just can't hear it. If I let them keep talking, I know exactly where my brain is going to go, and I just... I can't go back there. I spend so much energy just trying to build these walls around myself so I don't have to face it, but the walls keep getting smaller and smaller, and I'm just running out of places to hide.
Do you find yourself feeling depressed, guilty, or emotionally numb most days since your brother's accident?

Guilty doesn't even... I mean, yeah. Yes. But it’s not just guilt, and it's not exactly numbness either. It’s this... it’s this incredibly heavy mix of guilt and just pure, raw anger. And it's just sitting right here in my chest, all day long. Every single day, from the second I open my eyes in the morning until I finally manage to pass out at night, it's just this dead weight sitting right on my lungs. I'm just dragging it around with me everywhere I go, whether I'm on a job site or sitting in traffic in my truck. 

But it's the absolute worst when I'm at home. Especially... especially when I look at my nephew. I'll be in the kitchen, right? Maybe I'm just making some coffee or pouring him a bowl of cereal before he catches the bus. He's just sitting there at the counter, hunched over his phone or his homework, just... just being a kid, you know? A good kid who shouldn't have to be dealing with any of this mess. And I look over at him, and that weight in my chest just tightens up so hard I can barely breathe. Because all I can think about is how he lost his dad. He lost his actual father, the guy who was supposed to teach him how to drive, the guy who was supposed to see him graduate high school and get married. 

And instead of his dad... he got stuck with me. He got stuck living in my spare bedroom, with the guy who couldn't even keep his own brother alive. And I get so angry—angry at myself, angry at the whole damn situation—and then the guilt just swallows me whole because I'm looking at this boy whose life is completely shattered, and he has to rely on me now. I just stand there staring at him, feeling like an absolute fraud of a guardian, and it just eats at me all day long. I don't know how I'm ever supposed to get out from under that feeling, doc, I really don't. It just doesn't let up.
Have you noticed that your mood has been consistently low or that you've been more irritable than usual, even outside of the times when you're having these intrusive thoughts?

Irritable? Man, that's... that's putting it mildly. I used to be the guy on the site everyone wanted to work with because I had patience, you know? You're dealing with high voltage, you can't be a hothead, you have to keep your cool. But lately... lately it's like I'm just walking around with a lit fuse all the time, just waiting for a spark. It doesn't even take a big deal to set me off anymore. Just the littlest, stupidest things make me completely explode. 

Like at work, right? We've got this new apprentice on the crew. Kid's green as they come. And look, I know they have to learn, I was there once, I know how it is. But if he asks me the same question twice—like, I just spent ten minutes showing him exactly how to bend a piece of half-inch EMT conduit, and five minutes later he's asking me which way the shoe goes on the bender again—I just lose my absolute mind. I completely snap. I hear myself just yelling at the kid, cussing him up and down in front of the whole site, and it's like I'm watching myself do it from the outside, but I can't pull it back. I can't stop the words from coming out until I've already ripped his head off. 

And it's not just at the job site, which is the worst part. It's at home with my nephew, too. He'll do something totally normal for a teenager, right? Like he'll be fixing his bike or tinkering with something and he'll leave a couple of my tools out on the kitchen counter instead of putting them back in the chest where they belong. A year ago, I would've just tossed him a rag and said, "Hey bud, put your stuff away." But now? I see a socket wrench sitting next to the toaster and I just see red. I blow up at him, screaming about respect and responsibility, just dropping F-bombs over a piece of metal. And he just shrinks back and looks at me like I'm a monster, and I... I realize what I'm doing, but the anger is just so fast and so hot, I can't catch it before it ruins everything. It's like I'm just mad at the whole world, every single second of the day, and these people who don't deserve it are the ones paying the price for it.
When you have these intrusive thoughts or flashbacks, do you notice your body reacting physically—like your heart racing, sweating, or feeling on edge—like you're actually back in that moment?

Yeah, I mean... no, not really. I don't think so. I mean, my body doesn't really do all that stuff you're talking about, the sweating and the heart pounding and all that. It's more just... it's the thoughts, you know? The images. They just get stuck in my head on a loop, like a bad movie reel that just keeps playing the same scene over and over again, no matter how hard I try to shut it off. 

Like, I'll be driving down the highway, just minding my own business, maybe listening to the radio, trying to focus on the traffic, and then bam. Suddenly I'm not in my truck anymore. I'm right back there in that moment, seeing the flash, hearing the sound... but it's all in my head. It's not like my body is going crazy or anything. I'm not sitting there dripping in sweat or feeling like my chest is going to explode. I'm just... stuck. I'm stuck in the memory of it, and it's like my brain just hijacks everything else. 

And it's not just when I'm driving, either. It can happen anywhere. I could be at the grocery store, standing in the cereal aisle trying to decide between Cheerios and Frosted Flakes for my nephew, and suddenly I'm just paralyzed by this image of my brother. And I'm just standing there, staring at the boxes, completely lost in it. But if you were to look at me, you probably wouldn't even know anything was wrong. I probably just look like a guy who really can't make up his mind about breakfast. My hands aren't shaking, I'm not gasping for air... it's just this intense, overwhelming feeling of being trapped in that memory, like I'm drowning in it, but on the outside, I'm just standing still. So, yeah, I don't really get those physical reactions you mentioned, it's just... it's all up here, in my head, and it just won't stop.
Have you noticed that these feelings of guilt and anger have been constant, rather than just coming and going, since your brother's accident?

Constant? Yeah. Constant is exactly the word. There is no "coming and going" with this. It doesn't take a weekend off, it doesn't give me a break when I'm trying to sleep, it doesn't just fade into the background when I'm busy. It is just... there. Always. 

This has been going on for about four months now. Exactly four months, actually. Ever since the garage fire. I know you called it an accident, but... yeah, the fire. That's when all of this really started, and it hasn't let up for a single second since. It all started the exact same day my nephew came to live with us—well, with me. Right after the fire, we had to scramble, you know? I had to get the spare bedroom cleared out, move all my extra gear and boxes into the shed, and try to make it look like a place a teenager would actually want to sleep in, even though his whole world had just literally gone up in smoke. 

I remember that first night he was here, four months ago. I got him set up in the room, shut his door, and I walked into my own kitchen and just stood there in the dark. And that’s when it really hit me. The anger, the guilt, just dropping on me like a ton of bricks. And it hasn't left me since that night. Every time I look at the calendar, I just think, "another day, another week." It's been sixteen weeks of just waking up mad and going to bed feeling like the worst person on earth. I keep waiting for a day where I wake up and it feels even a little bit lighter, just a fraction of an ounce lighter, but it never does. So, no, it doesn't come and go. It's just my life now, every single day since that fire.

I'm right back there in that moment, seeing the flash, hearing the sound... but it's all in my head. It's not like my body is going crazy or anything. I'm not sitting there dripping in sweat or feeling like my chest is going to explode. I'm just... stuck. I'm stuck in the memory of it, and it's like my brain just hijacks everything else. 

And it's not just when I'm driving, either. It can happen anywhere. I could be at the grocery store, standing in the cereal aisle trying to decide between Cheerios and Frosted Flakes for my nephew, and suddenly I'm just paralyzed by this image of my brother. And I'm just standing there, staring at the boxes, completely lost in it. But if you were to look at me, you probably wouldn't even know anything was wrong. I probably just look like a guy who really can't make up his mind about breakfast. My hands aren't shaking, I'm not gasping for air... it's just this intense, overwhelming feeling of being trapped in that memory, like I'm drowning in it, but on the outside, I'm just standing still. So, yeah, I don't really get those physical reactions you mentioned, it's just... it's all up here, in my head, and it just won't stop.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences persistent negative emotional state (e.g., anger, guilt) as part of the PTSD criteria
doctor.question: Have you noticed that these feelings of guilt and anger have been constant, rather than just coming and going, since your brother's accident?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about four months, ever since the garage fire and my nephew coming to live with us.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the timeline and persistence of the symptoms since the accident, which corresponds to the duration of the patient's condition.

patient.answer:
Constant? Yeah. Constant is exactly the word. There is no "coming and going" with this. It doesn't take a weekend off, it doesn't give me a break when I'm trying to sleep, it doesn't just fade into the background when I'm busy. It is just... there. Always. 

This has been going on for about four months now. Exactly four months, actually. Ever since the garage fire. I know you called it an accident, but... yeah, the fire. That's when all of this really started, and it hasn't let up for a single second since. It all started the exact same day my nephew came to live with us—well, with me. Right after the fire, we had to scramble, you know? I had to get the spare bedroom cleared out, move all my extra gear and boxes into the shed, and try to make it look like a place a teenager would actually want to sleep in, even though his whole world had just literally gone up in smoke. 

I remember that first night he was here, four months ago. I got him set up in the room, shut his door, and I walked into my own kitchen and just stood there in the dark. And that’s when it really hit me. The anger, the guilt, just dropping on me like a ton of bricks. And it hasn't left me since that night. Every time I look at the calendar, I just think, "another day, another week." It's been sixteen weeks of just waking up mad and going to bed feeling like the worst person on earth. I keep waiting for a day where I wake up and it feels even a little bit lighter, just a fraction of an ounce lighter, but it never does. So, no, it doesn't come and go. It's just my life now, every single day since that fire.

inference.note: The patient's symptoms—persistent intrusive thoughts, flashbacks, emotional distress, avoidance behaviors, irritability, guilt, and constant negative mood—align with PTSD (F43.10). The absence of significant physical arousal during flashbacks rules out some anxiety-related conditions. The duration (>1 month) and onset following a traumatic event (brother's death in a fire) further support PTSD. Other candidates (F43.2x) are ruled out due to insufficient evidence of adjustment disorder with predominant depression or anxiety.
